# Computer, Browser, and Web {#sec-ch01}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[WEB 01 | Before we build a web game]{.game-title}

[Hardware]{.skill-chip} [Software]{.skill-chip} [Browser]{.skill-chip} [Web]{.skill-chip} [URL]{.skill-chip} [Server]{.skill-chip}

:::

## Overview {.unnumbered}

Before you build a web game, it helps to know **where the game lives**, **what runs it**, and **how the pieces reach the screen**.

A web game may look like one thing when you play it, but several parts work together behind the scenes. Your computer provides the hardware. Programs such as a browser provide the software. Files store the pictures, sounds, page information, and game instructions. The Web lets a browser request files from other computers when those files are not already on your own computer.

You do **not** need to memorize every technical word in this chapter. The goal is to build a simple picture in your mind. Later chapters will add HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to that picture one step at a time.

::: {.callout-note title="The big picture" icon="false"}
When you play a web game, you are usually using **software** called a browser on **hardware** such as a laptop or desktop computer. The browser opens game files from your computer or receives them from a server, then uses those files to show and run the game.
:::

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Computer hardware] --> B[Browser software]
    C[Game files] --> B
    B --> D[Web game on the screen]
```

**Read the picture:** The computer is the physical machine. The browser is a program running on that machine. The browser uses files to create the game experience you see.

## Our development flow: Structure → Style → Behavior {#sec-ch01-development-flow}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

The names tell you what to do: **build the structure** by deciding what belongs in the scene, **style** it so the player understands it, and **program game behavior** with operations and actions. Use this thinking strategy whenever you plan a page or game. A **scene** here means the page the player sees: its title, instructions, play area, characters or pictures, controls, and score. First decide what belongs in that scene and how its parts are grouped. Then choose how those parts look. Finally, decide what operations and actions should happen.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[1. Build the scene structure<br/>What belongs on the page?] --> B[2. Style the scene<br/>How should it look?]
    B --> C[3. Program game behavior<br/>What operations and actions happen?]
```

| Development step | Thinking question | Tool and example | Check before moving on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Build the scene structure | What does the player need to see or use? | HTML: a monster button, message, and score area | Each part exists and is in a sensible group and reading order. |
| 2. Style the scene | How can the player recognize and use those parts? | CSS: readable text, spacing, colors, button size | The scene is readable; its controls and play area are easy to find. |
| 3. Program game behavior | What should happen when the player acts or time passes? | JavaScript: remember a score, respond to a hit, move a star | Predict the result of one action, then compare it with the actual result. |

For example, plan **Robot Rescue** in this order: sketch a robot, an arena, a Start button, and a score; choose their sizes and colors; then describe actions such as starting, moving, collecting, and restarting. A drawing on paper is enough to begin the structure step.

This is our **development order**, not a promise about exactly when a browser loads each file. You will return to an earlier step when a new game action needs a new control or display. Build a small scene, style it, add one behavior, and check the result before expanding it.

Chapter 1 helps you plan these three steps. Chapter 2 builds structure and style and writes a behavior plan. Chapter 3 prepares JavaScript memory for the behavior step. Chapter 4 connects that memory to player actions.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- use the development flow **Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior** to plan a game;
- distinguish **hardware** from **software**;
- explain the difference between a **program**, a **file**, and a **folder**;
- explain what a **browser** does;
- distinguish the **Internet** from the **Web**;
- distinguish a **web page**, **website**, and **web game**;
- explain what a **URL** is and recognize its basic parts;
- describe the jobs of a **client** and a **server**;
- trace a simple **request and response** between a browser and a server;
- explain the difference between opening a **local file** and visiting a web address;
- describe, at a high level, where a web game can do its work.

## Hardware and software work together

Look at the computer in front of you. You may see a screen, keyboard, mouse, trackpad, and perhaps a desktop computer or laptop case. These are examples of **hardware**.

**Hardware** means the physical parts of a computer system---the parts that are built from electronic or mechanical components. You can usually touch hardware.

Examples include:

- a screen;
- a keyboard;
- a mouse or trackpad;
- a processor;
- memory;
- a storage drive;
- speakers.

Hardware by itself does not know how to open a website or run a game. It needs instructions. Those instructions are provided by **software**.

**Software** is a program, or a collection of programs and data, that tells computer hardware what work to do.

Examples include:

- a web browser such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari;
- a text editor used to write code;
- a drawing program;
- a music player;
- a web game running in a browser.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    C[Computer system]
    C --> H[Hardware<br/>physical parts]
    C --> S[Software<br/>programs and instructions]
    H --> H1[Screen]
    H --> H2[Keyboard]
    H --> H3[Storage]
    S --> S1[Browser]
    S --> S2[Text editor]
    S --> S3[Games]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch Out: A browser is not hardware" icon="false"}
Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari are **software**. The screen that shows the browser is hardware.
:::

### What is a program? {.unnumbered}

A **program** is a set of instructions that a computer can follow. A browser is a program. A calculator app is a program. A game is also a program.

When you start a program, the computer loads the instructions and begins carrying them out. Some programs open documents. Some programs play music. A browser opens and runs web content.

For this book, two programs will be especially important:

- A **text editor** lets you create and change code files.
- A **web browser** reads web files and shows the result.

You will spend a lot of time moving between these two programs: edit something, save it, return to the browser, and see what changed.

## Files and folders keep a project organized

Computers store information in **files**. A file can contain many kinds of information: words, pictures, music, video, data, or program instructions.

A **file name** helps you recognize a file. Many file names also end with a **file extension**, such as `.png` or `.txt`. The extension gives people and programs a clue about what kind of information the file contains.

A **folder** is a container used to organize files and other folders.

Think of a folder as a project box. If you make a space game, you want the files for that game to stay together instead of being scattered around your computer.

```text
space-game/
  index.html
  styles.css
  game.js
  images/
    spaceship.png
    planet.png
  sounds/
    launch.mp3
```

These are real web-project file names. `index.html` describes the page, `styles.css` describes its appearance, and `game.js` holds JavaScript instructions. The name `index.html` is a common starting-page name. An early example may keep all three kinds of code inside one HTML file; a larger project usually separates them.

| File category | Extensions used in this book | Browser's job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page | `.html` | Read the page structure and find its linked resources. |
| Stylesheet | `.css` | Apply colors, sizes, spacing, and layout rules. |
| Program | `.js` | Run the game instructions. |
| Picture | `.svg`, `.png` | Display an image or use it in a game drawing. |
| Sound | `.wav`, `.mp3` | Load audio that the game can play. |
| Data | `.json` | Read organized information, such as a level layout. |
| 3D model | `.glb` | Supply model data to the later 3D game code. |

The book itself is written in `.qmd` files. **Quarto** turns that manuscript into web pages for reading. When you build a game, you work with the game files above. A browser does not open a `.qmd` chapter as a playable game.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    A[space-game folder] --> B[Page file]
    A --> C[Style file]
    A --> D[Game program file]
    A --> E[images folder]
    A --> F[sounds folder]
    E --> G[spaceship.png]
    E --> H[planet.png]
    F --> I[launch.mp3]
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Try It: Find a file and its folder" icon="false"}
Open a folder on your computer. Pick one file and answer these questions:

1. What is the file's name?
2. Does it have a file extension?
3. Which folder contains it?
4. Which program would you use to open it?
:::

## The Internet and the Web are related, but they are not the same thing

People often use the words **Internet** and **Web** as if they mean the same thing. They are related, but they describe different ideas.

The **Internet** is a huge network that connects computers and devices around the world. It is the communication system that lets connected computers exchange information.

The **World Wide Web**, usually called the **Web**, is a system of pages and other resources that we access through the Internet, usually with a web browser.

One simple way to remember the difference is:

- **Internet:** the network that connects computers.
- **Web:** pages, sites, games, pictures, and other resources that browsers access using that network.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Your computer] --> B[Internet<br/>connects computers]
    B --> C[Web server]
    C --> D[Web pages and game files]
```

The Internet can be used for things other than the Web. The Web is one important service that uses the Internet.

::: {.callout-note title="A useful comparison" icon="false"}
Imagine roads connecting many towns. The **Internet** is like the road system. A **website** is like a place you can reach using those roads. A **browser** is one of the tools that helps you travel to and use that place.

The comparison is not perfect, but it can help you keep the words separate.
:::

## A browser is software that works with web resources

A **web browser** is software that helps you open and use web pages and web applications. Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari are examples.

A browser can get web files in two common ways:

1. It can open files that are already stored on your computer.
2. It can request files from another computer through a network.

After it receives the files, the browser uses them to create what you see and interact with on the screen.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    L[Files on your computer] -->|open| B[Browser]
    B --> S[What you see and use]
    W[Files from a web server] -->|receive| B
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch Out: The browser is not the Internet" icon="false"}
A browser is a program on your device. The Internet is the network connecting devices. You can even use a browser to open some local files when your computer is not connected to the Internet.
:::

### What happens when you type something in the address bar? {.unnumbered}

The long box near the top of a browser is usually called the **address bar**. You can use it to enter a web address. Browsers can also send words from the address bar to a search engine, so typing into the address bar does not always mean that you typed a web address.

When you enter a web address, the browser tries to find the resource at that address. If the resource is on another computer, the browser sends a request for it.

## Web pages, websites, and web games

These three terms are connected, but they do not mean exactly the same thing.

A **web page** is one page or view that a browser can display. A page might show instructions, a menu, a story, a score screen, or part of a game.

A **website** is a collection of related web pages and other files that belong together. A school website, news website, and game website may each contain many pages, images, and other resources.

A **web game** is a game designed to run through a web browser. It may use one page or several files. The browser may draw graphics, play sounds, read keyboard or mouse input, update scores, and run the rules of the game.

| Term | Simple meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web page | one page shown by a browser | a game's start screen |
| Website | related pages and resources | a game site with a home page, instructions, and games |
| Web game | a game that runs in a browser | a game where you move a character and collect stars |

::: {.callout-note title="Why this matters for our book" icon="false"}
The games in this book are **web games**. That means the browser is not just showing information. It will eventually run instructions that let the game react to clicks, keys, timers, collisions, and other events.
:::

## A URL tells a browser where to look

A **URL** is an address for a resource. URL stands for **Uniform Resource Locator**.

You can think of a URL as directions that help a browser locate something. That "something" might be a web page, an image, a game file, or another resource.

Here is a simple example:

```text
https://example.com/games/space-quest
```

For now, focus on three parts:

| Part | Example | What it tells us |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheme | `https://` | how the browser should communicate |
| Domain | `example.com` | which site or server name to contact |
| Path | `/games/space-quest` | which resource or location to ask for |

You do not need to memorize every possible URL part yet. The important idea is that a URL gives the browser an address it can use.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: A URL can contain more parts" icon="false"}
A URL can include additional information. For example:

```text
https://games.example.com:443/levels/maze?mode=easy#start
```

It may contain:

- a **scheme** such as `https`;
- a **host name** such as `games.example.com`;
- an optional **port** such as `443`;
- a **path** such as `/levels/maze`;
- an optional **query** such as `?mode=easy`;
- an optional **fragment** such as `#start`.

You will not need most of these pieces to begin making games. Return to them when a later project needs them.
:::

## Local files and web addresses

A browser does not always need to get a page from the Internet. It can also open a file stored directly on your computer.

A local file address may begin with `file:///`. For example:

```text
file:///Users/your-name/Documents/space-game/start.html
```

The important part is not the exact folder name. `file:///` tells you that the browser is opening a file from the local computer.

A web address often begins with `http://` or `https://`:

```text
https://example.com/games/space-quest
```

That normally tells the browser to contact a server through a network.

| Address begins with | Usual meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `file:///` | open a file stored on this computer |
| `http://` | request a web resource using HTTP |
| `https://` | request a web resource using encrypted HTTP communication |

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    B[Browser]
    L[Local file<br/>on your computer]
    I[Internet]
    S[Web server]
    L -->|open directly| B
    B -->|request| I
    I --> S
    S -->|response| I
    I --> B
```

**Read the picture:** A local file can go directly from storage on your computer to your browser. A web resource takes another route: the browser sends a request through the network and receives a response.

## Client and server describe jobs

When computers communicate, we often describe them by the job they are doing.

A **client** asks for or uses a service or resource. In this book, your browser often acts as a client because it asks for web files.

A **server** provides a service or resource. A web server can receive a request and send back a requested file or other data.

The words **client** and **server** describe roles. They do not always describe special kinds of hardware.

For example, your laptop is hardware. Chrome is software. When Chrome asks a web server for a page, Chrome is acting as a **client**.

A server also involves software. In everyday conversation, people sometimes use the word *server* for both the server program and the computer running that program. For now, remember the job: **a server responds to requests**.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser (client)
    participant S as Web server
    B->>S: Request a game file
    S-->>B: Send a response
    B->>B: Use the file
```

### Request and response {.unnumbered}

A **request** is a message asking for something.

A **response** is the answer that comes back.

For a web game, a simplified conversation might look like this:

> Browser: "Please send the game page."
>
> Server: "Here it is."
>
> Browser: "Now I need a picture used by the game."
>
> Server: "Here is that picture."

Real web communication contains more details, but this request-and-response idea is the foundation.

## Where does a web game do its work?

A web game can do a lot of work directly inside the browser. For example, the browser can respond when a player presses a key, move an object, update a score, draw graphics, and play sounds.

Some web games also communicate with servers. A server might help with jobs such as:

- saving an online account;
- storing a high score;
- loading shared game data;
- connecting several players.

A beginner game does not need all of those features. Many of the first games in this book can run mostly on your own computer in the browser.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    P[Player] -->|clicks and keys| B[Browser game]
    B -->|updates| G[Game screen]
    B -. optional requests .-> S[Server]
    S -. optional data .-> B
```

::: {.callout-note title="Client-side and server-side" icon="false"}
When work happens in the browser on the player's device, programmers often call it **client-side** work. When work happens in a server program, they call it **server-side** work.

You only need the basic idea now. Most of our early attention will stay on the browser side.
:::

## How HTML, CSS, and JavaScript fit together

You will write HTML and CSS in Chapter 2. First, recognize the three jobs that work together in our games:

- **HTML** describes the page's structure and content.
- **CSS** describes much of the page's appearance and layout.
- **JavaScript** gives the page programmable behavior.

Use them in our development flow: **HTML builds the scene structure → CSS gives it style → JavaScript supplies behaviors**. These three jobs let you build and check a game in manageable stages.

| Technology | Job in a future web game | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTML | what is on the page | a score area or game button |
| CSS | how it looks | size, spacing, color, position |
| JavaScript | what it does | increase the score after an action |

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    H[HTML<br/>Build the scene structure] --> C[CSS<br/>Style the scene]
    C --> J[JavaScript<br/>Program game behavior]
    J --> G[Web game]
```

Do not worry about the code yet. Chapter 2 begins with HTML and shows how a browser turns page structure into something you can see.

### The browser builds a page from connected files {.unnumbered}

The page file is the starting point. It can point to a stylesheet, pictures, and JavaScript files. The browser loads those resources, builds the page's structure, applies its styles, and runs its scripts. Loading a picture or a program may take time, so later games wait until their resources are ready.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    H[index.html] --> B[Browser builds page elements]
    C[styles.css] --> S[Browser styles the elements]
    B --> S
    S --> P[Page on the screen]
    J[game.js] --> R[Browser runs game instructions]
    R --> P
    A[Pictures, sounds, and models] --> P
```

The browser keeps a working representation of the page called the **Document Object Model**, or **DOM**. A heading, a button, and a score paragraph become elements in that representation. Chapter 2 gives some elements unique labels called **IDs**. Chapter 4 teaches JavaScript to find those elements and change them. Changing the page in the browser does not automatically change the saved HTML file.

### Recognize the page structures we will reuse {.unnumbered}

Our games grow in stages, but they keep familiar page parts: a title, instructions, a play area, controls, and a message or score. The play area changes as we learn new drawing techniques.

| Book stage | Structure to recognize | What HTML and CSS provide | What JavaScript adds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chapter 2: static website | Heading, sections, picture, list, player form | Content, labeled controls, a styled card | Game behavior comes later. |
| Chapters 3–5: Monster Clicker | Monster button, message, score paragraph | Visible elements with unique IDs | Chapter 3 stores data; Chapters 4–5 connect clicks and decisions. |
| Chapter 6: Monster Swarm | Container of buttons and a score span | Shared button classes and a flexible row | A loop connects the monsters. |
| Chapter 7: Catch the Star | Game-area container with a star inside | A sized box and coordinates for the star | Timers and clicks change its position. |
| Chapters 8–12: canvas games | Drawing surface, instructions, status, sometimes Restart | Canvas dimensions, frame, and page layout | Drawing, movement, collisions, and game rules |
| Chapters 13–16: complete 2D projects | Canvas, toolbar, choices, movement buttons, status, error area | A reusable game page and shared stylesheet | Modules load assets and run the game. |
| Chapters 17–20: 3D projects | A stage container plus the same controls and messages | Space for a canvas created by the renderer | Three.js draws the world; Rapier adds physics where needed. |

Use this table as a map. Chapter 2 explains the HTML and CSS vocabulary for these structures before Chapter 3 begins teaching JavaScript variables.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: What is a local web server?" icon="false"}
Later games in this book will use several JavaScript files, data files, or 3D models. For those projects, we will sometimes run a **local web server**.

A local server is server software running on your own computer. It may give your browser an address such as:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/
```

`127.0.0.1` is a special address that refers back to the same computer. Starting a local server for a project does **not** automatically publish that project to the Internet.

For now, you only need to recognize the idea. Later chapters will tell you when to use the local server and how to start it.
:::

Use **Structure → Style → Behavior** to connect these computer concepts to a future game. These are explanation and planning tasks; no game code is required.

6. A browser game

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

### Challenge 1: Explain a web game to a beginner

**Structure:** Describe the game page and the files it needs. **Style:** Explain that the browser uses visual rules to display those parts. **Behavior:** Describe which program carries out the game actions; use the requested vocabulary.

Imagine a friend says, "A web game is stored inside Chrome."

Write a short explanation that uses at least four of these words correctly:

**hardware, software, browser, file, Internet, Web, server, client**

### Challenge 2: Draw the journey of a game

**Structure:** Draw the browser and the two routes by which its scene files arrive. **Style:** Keep box labels and arrows readable. **Behavior:** Trace a request and response; explain how file delivery supports later game actions.

Draw a diagram showing two ways a browser can get game files:

1. from the same computer;
2. from a web server through the Internet.

Your diagram must include **browser**, **local file**, **request**, **response**, and **server**.

Then write two or three sentences explaining the difference between the two routes.

### Challenge 3: Plan a future game project

**Structure:** Sketch Robot Rescue and its project files. **Style:** Choose two visual decisions that help a player read the scene. **Behavior:** List three player actions and their expected results.

Imagine you will build a game called **Robot Rescue**. First sketch its **scene structure**: instructions, play area, robot, controls, and score. Next note two **style** choices. Then list three **behaviors**, each as an action and its expected result. Sketch a folder for the project. Include folders or files for at least:

- the game page;
- game instructions or code;
- images;
- sounds.

Use `index.html`, `styles.css`, and `game.js` for the three web-code files, then choose meaningful names for your pictures and sounds.

Then answer: **Why is keeping related game files in one project folder useful?**

### Challenge 4: Local game or online game?

**Structure:** Identify the maze, controls, and score in each game plan. **Style:** Keep the scene legible in both plans; server location does not choose its colors. **Behavior:** Decide which actions and saved/shared data need browser or server work.

You are designing two games:

- **Game A** is a simple maze that runs on one student's laptop.
- **Game B** lets students on different computers compare high scores online.

For each game, explain which work could happen in the browser and whether a server would be useful. You do not need to design the server; explain only the jobs it might perform.

### Challenge 5: Trace the development flow

**Structure:** Identify the treasure, Collect control, and score. **Style:** Identify the task that changes how those existing parts look. **Behavior:** Identify the task that connects collection to a score update, then order all three tasks.

A friend wants to make a treasure game. Put these development tasks in order and name their stages:

- choose colors and spacing so the treasure is easy to see;
- create a treasure picture, a Collect button, and a score area;
- make Collect increase the score.

Then explain why changing a picture's color does not, by itself, make collecting it increase the score.
